articles.title: Stunning collection of prehistoric engravings found in Spanish cave
articles.summary: A close examination of a frequently visited cave wall in Spain has revealed a spectacular assembly of rock art engravings thought to be at least 19,000 years old
articles.content:
A close examination of a frequently visited cave wall in Spain has revealed a spectacular assembly of rock art engravings thought to be at least 19,000 years old

Palaeolithic depiction of a horse at Cova de la Font Major, a cave in Spain Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, Míriam Salas-Altès

A gallery of hundreds of engraved motifs and dozens of prehistoric animal images has been found in a cave in Spain, where they had gone unnoticed despite the cave being a popular tourist attraction.

Josep Maria Vergès at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology stumbled on the rock art at Cova de la Font Major, west of Barcelona, after a tourist group caught his attention.

The visitors, wearing wetsuits, were taking part in an adventure activity and had emerged from a nearby opening that led into a small side gallery. “Since it was my first time working at the site and I was unfamiliar with this side gallery, I went to take a look,” says Vergès.

Advertisement

Upon entering, he saw that the walls were covered with names and dates engraved by people who had passed through the gallery since 1957. To examine them more closely, he removed his helmet and used the headlamp to illuminate the wall with raking light – a technique used to observe engravings because it creates shadows in the incised grooves.

“Almost immediately, among the modern graffiti, I noticed a series of vertical lines that appeared ancient,” says Vergès. “I moved slightly and spotted another one. Then, as I turned toward the opposite wall and shone the light across its surface, the horse appeared and I realised it was executed in a Palaeolithic style.”

He also immediately discovered that there were “many more engravings, many of them figurative representations of different animals”, he says.

Representation of a bear with ears, shown in frontal perspective and with a slightly open mouth Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, Míriam Salas-Altès

So far, 280 motifs have been discovered in the gallery, including 55 animal figures, making the cave one of the richest and most important archaeological finds along the Iberian coast between the Pyrenees and Gibraltar.

One challenge for archaeologists is that it is extremely difficult to date the engravings themselves, but human occupation in the cave has been dated to between 26,000 and 41,000 years ago and, based on the style, the art is likely to be over 19,000 years old.

Team member Míriam Salas-Altès, also at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, says one of the most outstanding figures is a hind, or adult female deer, depicted with its head lowered, its muzzle extending across a natural fissure.

The crack appears to have been deliberately incorporated into the composition as the surface of a body of water from which the hind is drinking. “If this hypothesis is correct, the scene would constitute one of the earliest known representations of water in human artistic expression,” she says.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

Among the non-figurative engravings, the team identified groups of lines arranged in twos, threes or fours and, in some cases, series of up to 40 straight, parallel lines, as well as Y-shaped signs and circular or semicircular shapes. “As for what they represent, that question has led to dozens of different theories,” says Vergès. “Unfortunately, the code needed to understand its message has not fossilised.”

Paul Taçon at Griffith University in Australia says the discovery fills a large gap in our knowledge of the distribution of Palaeolithic art in western Europe. While the exact age of the rock art is yet to be determined, it is “obvious” that it was made by a Palaeolithic culture, he says.

“It is exciting that new discoveries at long-visited sites are revealing ancient evidence of a very early painting tradition,” says Taçon.

articles.personality_title: Ancient animal engravings discovered in a Spanish cave
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – A well-known cave in Spain, visited by many tourists, was recently studied more closely by archaeologists. This cave is located west of Barcelona and has been known for signs of human presence thousands of years ago.

**What happened** – Josep Maria Vergès from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology found hundreds of ancient engravings on the cave walls. These include 55 images of animals like horses, bears, and deer. The art was hidden among modern graffiti but became visible when Vergès used special lighting. The drawings are thought to be at least 19,000 years old.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it adds a large and detailed collection of prehistoric art to what we know about early humans in Europe. One unique engraving shows a deer drinking water, using a natural crack in the rock to represent the water, which might be one of the earliest water images made by humans. This helps us understand how early people expressed their world through art.

**What's next step** – Scientists will work to date the engravings more precisely and study the different shapes and signs found alongside the animals. This could reveal more about the meaning and purpose of the art and the people who made it.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A rich collection of 19,000-year-old animal engravings found in a Spanish cave offers new clues about early human creativity and life.
articles.personality_title_fr: Découverte de gravures animales anciennes dans une grotte espagnole
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Une grotte bien connue en Espagne, souvent visitée par des touristes, a été récemment étudiée de plus près par des archéologues. Cette grotte se trouve à l'ouest de Barcelone et montre des traces de présence humaine datant de plusieurs milliers d'années.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Josep Maria Vergès de l'Institut catalan de paléoécologie humaine a découvert des centaines de gravures anciennes sur les murs de la grotte. Parmi elles, 55 images d'animaux comme des chevaux, des ours et des cerfs. Ces dessins étaient cachés parmi des graffitis modernes, mais sont devenus visibles grâce à un éclairage spécial. L'art daterait d'au moins 19 000 ans.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle ajoute une grande collection détaillée d'art préhistorique à notre connaissance des premiers humains en Europe. Une gravure unique montre un cerf buvant de l'eau, utilisant une fissure naturelle dans la roche pour représenter l'eau, ce qui pourrait être l'une des premières images d'eau réalisées par des humains. Cela aide à comprendre comment les premiers hommes exprimaient leur monde à travers l'art.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont chercher à dater plus précisément les gravures et étudier les différentes formes et signes trouvés avec les animaux. Cela pourrait révéler davantage sur la signification et l'objectif de cet art et des personnes qui l'ont créé.

**Phrase clé** – Une riche collection de gravures animales vieilles de 19 000 ans découverte dans une grotte espagnole offre de nouveaux indices sur la créativité et la vie des premiers humains.
articles.personality_title_es: Descubren grabados animales antiguos en una cueva española
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Una cueva muy conocida en España, visitada por muchos turistas, fue estudiada más de cerca recientemente por arqueólogos. Esta cueva está situada al oeste de Barcelona y se sabe que hubo presencia humana hace miles de años.

**Qué pasó** – Josep Maria Vergès del Instituto Catalán de Paleoecología Humana encontró cientos de grabados antiguos en las paredes de la cueva. Incluyen 55 imágenes de animales como caballos, osos y ciervos. El arte estaba oculto entre grafitis modernos, pero se hizo visible al usar una luz especial. Se cree que las imágenes tienen al menos 19,000 años.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque añade una gran y detallada colección de arte prehistórico a lo que sabemos sobre los primeros humanos en Europa. Un grabado único muestra un ciervo bebiendo agua, usando una grieta natural en la roca para representar el agua, lo que podría ser una de las primeras imágenes de agua hechas por humanos. Esto ayuda a entender cómo las personas antiguas expresaban su mundo a través del arte.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos trabajarán para fechar con más precisión los grabados y estudiar las diferentes formas y signos encontrados junto a los animales. Esto podría revelar más sobre el significado y propósito del arte y de quienes lo hicieron.

**Frase clave** – Una rica colección de grabados animales de hace 19,000 años encontrada en una cueva española ofrece nuevas pistas sobre la creatividad y vida de los primeros humanos.
articles.image_prompt: A warm, detailed painting of an ancient cave interior softly illuminated by raking light, revealing delicate Palaeolithic-style engravings of a horse, a bear, and a hind deer drinking from a natural fissure resembling water, surrounded by intricate abstract line motifs etched into textured stone walls in natural earthy tones.
